notes.title: Grammar in this lesson
notes.pattern: Vる時 / Nの時 / Nの後
notes.explanation: 時 is read とき when it means a time or occasion; it differs from the clock counter 時, read じ. A noun uses の before 時: 子供の時. 後, read あと, means afterward. 暇 is free time or being unoccupied.

notes.title: When you do something
notes.explanation: Use the dictionary form before 時: 読みます becomes 読む, so 本を読む時 means “when I read a book”. Keep 本を with its verb. The whole expression tells when you use your glasses. A plain verb can also describe a following noun; Japanese does not insert “that” or “which”.

notes.title: Grammar in this lesson
notes.pattern: Nました / 久しぶりにVました
notes.explanation: さっき refers to a short time ago; 最近 covers a recent period. この間 means the other day. 昨夜 is read ゆうべ here. 久しぶりに describes doing something after a long interval. 今度 can mean this time or next time; 今回 refers to this occasion.

notes.title: The book I bought
notes.explanation: Before a noun, use a plain verb form. For a completed purchase, 買う becomes 買った, not 買いました: 買った本 is “the book I bought”. この間 tells when you bought it. The final です keeps the whole sentence polite. Other verbs have their own plain past forms.

notes.title: Grammar in this lesson
notes.pattern: どなた / ご存知ですか / Nを紹介します
notes.explanation: どなた is a polite who. ご存知ですか respectfully asks whether the listener knows something; do not use ご存知 to describe your own knowledge. 者, read もの here, is a formal way to refer to a person, often yourself in a self-description.

notes.title: Describe what someone is doing
notes.explanation: Inside a noun-modifying clause, use ている instead of polite ています. 勉強している者 is someone who is studying.

notes.title: A polite lead-in
notes.pattern: 失礼ですが、どなたですか
notes.explanation: が after a complete statement can lead into a contrasting statement or soften a question. Here 失礼ですが politely leads into asking who someone is.

notes.title: Grammar in this lesson
notes.pattern: おっしゃいます / なさいます / 召し上がります / くださいます
notes.explanation: These verbs respectfully describe the other person’s actions. おっしゃる replaces 言う, なさる replaces する, and 召し上がる replaces 食べる or 飲む. くださる describes someone giving to you respectfully. Its polite form is くださいます, not くださります.

notes.title: Report what someone says
notes.explanation: と marks the content of speech or thought. A reported statement uses a plain clause; a noun statement ends in だ: 学生だと言いました. An exact quotation keeps the words as spoken, including polite endings. 何とおっしゃいましたか asks what the person said.

notes.title: Grammar in this lesson
notes.explanation: After a て-form, くださいます respectfully describes someone doing something for you or your group. It is the respectful counterpart of くれます.

notes.pattern: さあ / なんで / いや / plain endings
notes.explanation: 行かない is the plain negative of 行く, and 来なかった the plain past negative of 来る; のですか asks for an explanation. さあ can encourage the next action; まあ can soften a reaction. なんで is conversational why, and いや can introduce a correction. お前 and ばか can be rude or insulting. Learn to recognize them in dialogue; use あなた, a name, or an omitted subject in polite interaction, and avoid calling people ばか.

notes.title: Grammar in this lesson
notes.pattern: さらに / 少なくとも / あらゆるN / いずれ
notes.explanation: さらに adds more; 少なくとも gives a minimum. あらゆる means every possible kind, and 唯一 the only one. 存在 is existence, while 無 means nothingness or absence; 無にする makes an effort come to nothing. いずれ can mean eventually. ただ may mean only or free of charge. とにかく and さて move a conversation forward in different ways: anyway, and now then.

だ: plain copula; used before と in a quoted thought
／: change of speaker in a short dialogue
日: day counter; special readings are taught separately
ではありませんでした: でわありませんでした
という: called; identifies a name or a word before a noun
ために: for the sake of; for the purpose of
とも: both; all of the stated number
ほう: side or alternative in a comparison
そうです: looks or seems; after an adjective stem
だったら: if it is; hypothetical condition after a noun
